lines.text: love. And one thing alone can save us from the world and
from ourselves: that we truly place ourselves before God as
the One who alone has the right to judge us, who overthrows
the verdict of our own self-examination by His judgment
which humbles us far more deeply than our own, because it
is the judgment of love which is spoken to us in Jesus. "My
peace I leave with you. My peace I give to you. Not as the
world gives, give I to you. Let not your hearts be troubled,
neither let them be afraid."
IV
Our disquiet and distress in the midst of the world spring
however not only from our own personal conduct, but also
from the fate in which we are involved, however character-
istically our conduct and our fate may be intertwined. Our
meditation this evening must consist not only in reflecting
about ourselves, but also in reflecting about the world in
which we are placed. For it is just as we consider the
surrounding world that we need the promise: "My peace
I give to you."
For is it possible to carry on our work without again and
again being irritated and disturbed by the distress and
dispeace which prevail in this world in which we are so
deeply involved? Who could remain unmoved in face of the
calamity which has overtaken millions of men, our brothers
in the Far East? And who must not be filled with continuing
pain and indignation on hearing of the injustice and violence,
of the sacrifices which have been and still are, here and there,
the awful consequences of political revolution? Which of us
has not been oppressed by the sufferings of the Church, and
which of us this evening can fail to think of the troubles that
have disturbed the intimate circle of our studies and of those
who have been, directly or indirectly, affected? Can we
preserve our inner peace in the midst of all this tormenting
unrest and disturbance? In fact, ought we to try so to do?
